status: One unchanged shared trade claim reused for B3.9 through actual dated Canadian economic effects and its complete existing evidence. No country-specific trade topic or claim widening.

claimReview.wholeClaim: Why countries trade; own-country imports/exports; goods moving internationally; different currencies and exchange when travelling.
claimReview.readiness: The retained hard How the Economy Works prerequisite supports producers/consumers and price reasoning. No dependency change, full advanced economic inventory or new arithmetic requirement is added.
claimReview.intervalBoundary: Add only an exact 11–12 Social Studies context. Preserve the historical 11–13 Maths context and all other intervals; the old Grade 7 code is not new primary authoring.

trade.locator: Actual 1.1 sector narrative and 2.2 United States body/Figure 12 text;2025 data, retrievedbyGAC 5 May 2026
trade.scope: Merchandise goods, values and stated drivers; not all services, individual household incomes or a permanent future forecast.

bilateral.scope: An attributed Canadian governmental account of the relationship; employment figures are not a measure of each family’s gain.

currency.locator: Actual rate definition and dated 10 November 2026 US dollar row
currency.scope: Indicative daily average, not a guaranteed retail transaction rate or financial advice.

facts: In 2025 Canadian goods exports to the United States fell 5.3%; goods imports from it fell 4.2%.

Energy export receipts fell as oil prices and volumes declined. Motor vehicles/parts exports and imports also fell; the account relates these changes to trade-policy changes and integrated production.
Canada both exported goods such as energy products and vehicles/parts and imported vehicles/parts and other products. A change in dollar value can reflect prices as well as physical quantities.
limits: These are2025 observations, not a claim all trade always falls or every household lost the same amount.
The report’s appendix total-import figure conflicts with its overview; no disputed total is used.

facts: Canada and the United States share cross-border supply chains and energy infrastructure. The governmental account describes trade/investment as supporting work on both sides.
Selling abroad connects Canadian producers to customers; buying abroad supplies goods and components. Neither an import nor an export is automatically a net harm or benefit for every person.
limits: Do not infer a specific worker’s job loss, wage or household effect from aggregate export values.

facts: Canadian and US dollars are different currencies. The Bank’s10 November 2026 indicative average expressed 1 US dollar as 1.4181 Canadian dollars.
A Canadian traveller may need to exchange Canadian dollars for another currency. Fees and the actual offered rate can differ; arithmetic conversion is optional here.
limits: This is an explicitly dated illustration, not a current travel quote or an assumption every country has a unique currency.

learnerActions: Adult setup: provide original concise fact cards, an imports-to-Canada/exports-from-Canada goods route diagram and the dated currency example; retain the stated goods/value/period limits.

Explain why a country trades rather than obtains every good locally. Give one actual Canadian import and export from the packet and follow their directions across the border; identify producer/customer or component use.

Describe a significant observed 2025 economic effect on Canada: lower receipts from the selected exports and changed cross-border vehicle/parts trade. Use the source’s price/quantity and policy/production explanation, rather than claim the number alone proves one cause or each family’s experience.

Explain that a purchase abroad may involve a different currency and exchange; distinguish the US dollar from the Canadian dollar using the supplied date/definition, without requiring decimal-rate computation.

Transfer to this original hypothetical case: a Canadian factory buys a component abroad and sells some finished products overseas. Explain both import/export links and one plausible consequence if a route is interrupted; label it a modelled consequence, not another observed 2025 event.
successConditions: Actual Canadian import/export directions and reasons are correct.
At least one significant actual Canadian economic effect is explained from the dated source and does not confuse dollar values with quantities or infer individual welfare.
The unchanged claim’s currency/exchange and goods-route requirements are accounted for, rather than only the new source’s effect.
nearMisses: Calls imported vehicles Canadian exports or says every dollar of imports is a national loss.
Treats a lower dollar value as proof of exactly the same proportional fall in physical goods or jobs.
Gives a generic economic definition but cannot describe an actual sourced Canadian effect.

coverageBoundary: B3.9 has source-fit authoring coverage. Wider B3.6 political/social interactions, B3.8 partner-selection reasons and country/city mapping remain separately reviewed; no whole-B completion or learner attainment is inferred.
